newsitem.title: USA: Dole looks for votes in New Jersey, a swing state.
newsitem.headline: Dole looks for votes in New Jersey, a swing state.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole took his "Asphalt One" bus tour through New Jersey on Tuesday but his two-day investment in this battleground state was chased by dark clouds and the threat of remnants of a tropical storm.
"All Democrats, get on board," Dole quipped over the microphone from his campaign bus, dubbed "Asphalt One," a play on the presidential jet, Air Force One.

The first of five scheduled outdoor rallies in New Jersey, in the town of Lyndhurst, was sparsely attended, and Dole spoke only briefly. But he made time in his schedule to add a stop at a colourful highway diner where he was sure to find lots of people and have the kind of chats that would generate favourable television coverage.

Dole planned an intensive two-day trip through New Jersey, a swing state with 15 electoral votes that backed President Bill Clinton in 1992 and where various opinion polls show Clinton has an edge of between 12 and 28 percentage points.

Nationally, the latest tracking poll for Reuters by the Zogby Group International released on Tuesday found the race had narrowed considerably to a 5.3 percentage point margin. Clinton had 43.8 percent to Dole's 38.5 among 900 likely voters. Ross Perot had 4.5 and 11.3 percent were undecided.

At the rally at a damp park, Dole stressed his themes of cutting taxes and fighting illegal drugs. He pushed the message of his Sunday debate against Clinton, depicting himself as a man of his word in contrast with an unreliable Democrat who makes "empty promises."
"My word is good, I'll keep my promises to the American people," Dole said. "I can give you example after example of Clinton saying one thing and then did another," he said.
"When Bob Dole gives you his word you can go to the bank with it, he won't change his mind."

Dole has boasted of trying to stick to issues and avoiding name-calling but he could not resist picking up a cue from one boisterous supporter who reached out to shake his hand and shouted, "Please get Bozo out of the White House."
"Bozo's on his way out," replied Dole.

After a fairly upbeat first day of the bus tour on the morning after the first presidential debate, where Dole was largely seen as doing better than many anticipated, Tuesday dawned gray and misty as a storm raced up the East Coast.

At the first rally, Dole stuck to an abbreviated version of his stump speech, speaking for only about 10 minutes. He reviewed his plan for an across-the-board 15 percent tax cut and explained how his tax policy would help families with young children, calling them "little tax credits."
"This is not a Wall Street tax cut," he said, as he had during Sunday's debate. "This is a family tax cut."
